newsitem.title: USA: CME to launch fresh pork belly contracts Friday.
newsitem.headline: CME to launch fresh pork belly contracts Friday.

text.p: The new Chicago Mercantile Exchange fresh pork belly contact will make its inaugural trade on Friday, but will likely be lightly traded until open interest builds for the distant contracts.

"The industry is very much in favor of this contract -- it is what they have been wanting for some time and I think it will be well received," said Marshall Stein, chairman of the CME Pork Products committee.
September and November 1998 and January 1999 fresh contracts will be listed for the first day of trade on Friday.
The initial open will be the same time as frozen, 0910 CST/1510 GMT.

But Stein said that it will take time to build a large following because the first delivery for the new contract is nearly two years away and there is still another year of the frozen contract to go. That last year of frozen contracts has just recently started to build open interest.
The bacon business has been changing over the years and there is more demand for fresh product and less for stored frozen bellies, industry sources said.
The new contract will be cash settled, a departure from the old delivery system, Stein noted.
"As the hogs have shown us how efficient and effective cash settlement can be, we hope to have a similar experience in the pork bellies," Stein added.
But not all market watchers are certain the change in contract specifications will be beneficial in reducing the exceptional number of limit moves the contract has become famous for.

The exchange previously tackled that issue by increasing the daily limit in the pork belly pit to three cents a lb from two cents. The move has reduced the number of times futures have locked the daily limit somewhat.
"The problem I see with the new contract is what incentive anybody is going to have to store bellies," said Rich Tokheim, president of Investment Research Company.

Tokheim said there will be no way to have a solid hedge which could boost volatility instead of lowering it as some had hoped. When there are too many bellies around and no place to store them, cash prices will drop and when demand is up and there are no frozen bellies in storage, prices will jump, he said.
"At first I thought, just like everybody else, this (new contract) was going to reduce the volatility - now I'm leaning the other way," Tokheim added.
